chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad, all from Ibn Mahboub, from Khalid ibn Jarir, from Abu Al-Rabie Al-Shamy, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the origin of wine, how its permissibility began and its prohibition, and when wine was taken. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, when Adam (peace be upon him) descended from Paradise, he desired from its fruits. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down to him two branches of grapes, so he planted them. When they grew leaves and bore fruit and became large, Iblees (may Allah curse him) came and built a wall around them. Adam (peace be upon him) said: What is your state, O Accursed? Iblees said: These two are mine. He said to him: You are lying!'

So they both agreed to have the Holy Spirit decide between them. When they went to him, Adam (peace be upon him) related his story to him. The Holy Spirit took a bundle of fire and threw it upon them, with the grapes still in their branches, to the extent that Adam (peace be upon him) thought that nothing remained of them, and Iblees (may Allah curse him) thought the same.

He said: So the fire entered where it entered, and two-thirds of them had gone (burned), and one-third remained. So the Spirit said: As for what went from them, that is the share of Iblees (may Allah curse him), and whatever remains is for you, O Adam.
Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Khalid ibn Nafi', from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) — similar to it.
ai.seo_question: What is the origin story of wine in Shia hadith literature?
ai.summary: This narrative from *Al-Kafi* presents a unique cosmological account where the origin of wine is linked to the Fall of Adam, detailing a dispute with Iblees resolved by the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) who consumed two-thirds of the grapevines, leaving one-third for humanity. In Shia scholarly tradition, this story serves as a metaphysical explanation for the inherent duality of wine—its initial permissibility evolving into prohibition—and underscores the role of the Holy Spirit in mediating divine decrees regarding earthly sustenance. It highlights the transition from a state of natural allowance to specific legal restriction, framing wine's history within the broader narrative of human descent and spiritual trial.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father and a number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad and Sahl Bin Ziyad, altogether from Ibn Mahboub, from Khalid Bin Jareer, from Abu Al Rabie Al Shamy who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the origin of the wine, how did its permissibility begin, and its Prohibition, and when was the wine taken?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘When Adam<sup>as</sup> descended from the Paradise, he<sup>asws</sup> desired from its fruits. So Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic Sent down two branches of grapes unto him<sup>as</sup>. So he<sup>as</sup> planted these. So when it grew leaves, and fruits, and became big, Iblees<sup>la</sup> may Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Curse him<sup>la</sup>, came over. So he<sup>la</sup> built a wall over these. So Adam<sup>as</sup> said: ‘What is your<sup>la</sup> state, O Accursed?’ So Iblees<sup>la</sup> said, ‘These two are mine<sup>la</sup>’. So he<sup>as</sup> said: ‘You<sup>la</sup> are lying!’

So they both agreed for the Holy Spirit to (decide) between them. So when they both ended up to it, Adam<sup>as</sup> related his<sup>as</sup> story to him, and the Holy Spirit took some fire and threw it upon both (trees), and the grapes were in their branches, to the extent that Adam<sup>as</sup> thought that there would not remain anything from these, and Iblees<sup>la</sup>, may Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Curse him<sup>la</sup>, thought similar to that.

He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘So the fire entered wherever it tends to enter, and two thirds from these two (trees) had gone away (incinerated), and there remained a third. So the (Holy) Spirit said: ‘As for what has gone from these two, so it is the share of Iblees<sup>la</sup>, may Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Curse him<sup>la</sup>, and whatever remains, so it is for you<sup>as</sup>, O Adam<sup>as</sup>’.
Al-Hassan Bin Mahboub, from Khalid Bin Nafi’n, from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> – similar to it’.
en.sarwar: 1. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father and a number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad all from ibn Mahbub from Khalid ibn Jarir from abu al-Rabi’ al-Shamiy who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the origin of wine and how in the beginning it was lawful and its unlawfulness and when it was found. He (the Imam) said, ‘When Adam, ‘Alayhi al- Salam, descended from the garden (paradises) he desired its fruits; and Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, sent him two twigs of grape vine which he planted. When they grew leaves and fruits came out and ripened, Satan, may Allah condemn him built a wall around them. Adam, ‘Alayhi al-Salam asked how is your condition, O condemned one?’ He said, ‘They are for me.’ He said, ‘You are lying.’

They agreed to go for Judgment before the Holy spirit. When they arrived before him, Adam, ‘Alayhi al-Salam told his side of the story. The holy spirit took a certain amount of fire and threw it on them, when there were grapes on their branches. Adam, ‘Alayhi al-Salam thought that nothing is left from them and so also thought Satan, may Allah condemn him.’

He (the Imam) said, ‘The fire worked as it did but two-third were gone and one-third was left. The Holy Spirit said, ‘Whatever is gone is the share of Iblis, may Allah condemn him, and what is left is the share of Adam, ‘Alayhi al-Salam.’”
Al-Hassan ibn Mahbub has narrated from Khalid ibn Nafi’ from abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has narrated a similar Hadith.
